disease_info: Persistent Depressive Disorder (dysthymia) is a chronic mood disorder characterized by a consistently low or dysthymic mood lasting at least two years in adults, with no extended periods of full remission. Individuals often function day-to-day but at a reduced level, experiencing a long-standing sense of gloom, low motivation, and other depressive features that become part of their perceived personality. Clinically, it differs from major depressive disorder by its chronicity and typically milder, more insidious presentation, though episodes of major depression can occur on top of it ("double depression"). It is frequently under-recognized because patients and families may attribute the symptoms to character or life circumstances rather than a treatable illness, and impairment is often seen in social, occupational, or academic domains over time.

narrative.stressor: About three years ago, Lan took on a particularly demanding caseload when her agency lost two senior aides, leaving her covering more medically fragile, homebound elders with minimal backup. Around the same time, her mother in the South Bay began to decline with worsening diabetes and mobility issues, and Lan found herself driving down on weekends to coordinate appointments and manage her mother’s care, on top of her full-time job and community volunteering. Over the following 2-plus years, the combination of emotional labor at work, worry about her mother, and a gradual pulling back from her usual art, hiking, and cultural activities eroded her sense of balance and satisfaction, though she kept telling herself this was just what a devoted daughter and caregiver does. She finally agreed to see her primary care doctor after her husband and a younger aide she mentors both commented that she seemed to have lost her usual enthusiasm for patients and had started turning down museum outings and senior-center workshops that once energized her, prompting her provider to refer her for a psychiatric evaluation.
narrative.chief_complaint: I feel like I’ve been stuck in this low, heavy mood for years and I just don’t enjoy anything the way I used to.

narrative.stressor: Clifford began a phased retirement a little over three years ago, shifting from full-time IT leadership to a part-time advisory role and then officially retiring sooner than he had planned when his company restructured. At first he welcomed the chance to fish more and tend his garden, but as months passed he struggled to find a sense of purpose comparable to managing complex systems and mentoring younger staff, and he became increasingly preoccupied with whether he was still useful or "keeping up" with rapid changes in technology. Over the next 2 years and 4 months, he gradually withdrew from some community activities, started missing routine appointments, and found that even tinkering with vintage hardware and volunteering with the youth robotics club felt more like obligations than sources of satisfaction, yet he downplayed this as just getting older. His wife eventually insisted he bring it up at a checkup after he mentioned that most days felt like he was just going through the motions and that even planning simple road trips or attending church concerts seemed like more effort than they were worth, leading to a referral for mental health evaluation.
narrative.chief_complaint: I’m just tired all the time and don’t have the energy to do much of anything anymore, even the stuff I used to enjoy.

narrative.stressor: For Nikeita, the difficulties started after she transitioned from full-time college coursework into a demanding QA inspector job on rotating shifts while continuing part-time classes about two and a half years ago. Initially energized by the responsibility and the steady paycheck, she gradually found that the irregular hours, constant attention to production quotas, and pressure to prove herself as one of the youngest on the line left little time or energy for basketball league games, dancing nights, or STEM volunteering that used to ground her. Over the next 2 years and 4 months, this imbalance slowly became her new normal: she kept up appearances with friends but often skipped practices or social events at the last minute, blaming work or school, and told herself she just needed to "push through" until she could move up to a better role. She finally sought help after a supervisor commented on her reduced engagement and a close friend from church pointed out that she hadn’t seemed like her usual upbeat, competitive self for a long time, which made her realize how long she had been feeling this way and prompted her to ask her campus health clinic for a mental health referral.
narrative.chief_complaint: My sleep has been messed up for a long time, and no matter how I change my schedule I can’t seem to get any real rest.
